description: OrbitAI Innovators is an interdisciplinary team participating in the NASA Space Apps Challenge. We are passionate about leveraging Artificial Intelligence, Machine Learning, Data Science, and modern Software Engineering to build practical, scalable, and data-driven solutions for Earth and space exploration challenges.
summary: OrbitAI Copilot is an offline, explainable AI health monitor for astronauts on long-duration missions. On Mars, radio delay can reach 20+ minutes, so crews cannot depend on ground control to spot slow health trends. Our copilot learns each astronaut's personal baseline, detects drift in heart rate, HRV, SpO2, temperature, sleep, exercise, mood and radiation exposure, scores cardiovascular, bone/muscle, immune and behavioral risk from 0 to 100, and gives plain-language advice with the reason for every alert. It runs fully onboard with no internet.
details:
Challenge: Crew Health Monitoring for Astronauts on Space Missions.

 

Problem. Long-duration missions expose astronauts to radiation, isolation, confinement, altered gravity and a hostile closed environment. These cause immune changes, bone loss, cardiovascular events and behavioral health problems. On a Mars mission, one-way communication delay is roughly 4 to 24 minutes, so astronauts carry much of the responsibility for their own health, yet nobody can watch every signal every day.

 

Solution. OrbitAI Copilot is a Python/Streamlit application that works as an onboard health copilot:

1. Personal baseline: the first 14 mission days establish each astronaut's own normal for resting heart rate, HRV, SpO2, skin temperature, sleep, exercise minutes and daily mood check-in.

2. Anomaly detection: a 3-day rolling z-score compares recent data with the astronaut's own baseline. We chose explainable statistics over a black box so a crew member can trust and verify every alert.

3. Risk scoring: weighted scores (0-100) for Cardiovascular, Bone/Muscle, Immune and Behavioral risk, matching the four risks named in the challenge. Cumulative radiation dose is tracked against NASA's 600 mSv career limit, and solar particle events trigger an immediate storm-shelter alert.

4. Plain-language advice: each alert states what to do and why it was flagged (for example, "HRV 3.1σ below baseline, sleep 2.0σ below baseline").

5. Dashboard: crew overview, per-astronaut risk cards, trend charts with the personal normal band, and a downloadable report.

 

Demo scenarios (simulated, 4 crew members, 90 days): slow stress and cardiovascular drift (Dr. Chen), exercise equipment failure causing bone/muscle load loss (Eng. Ruiz), and a solar particle event followed by early immune signs (Spec. Okafor). A healthy control (Cdr. Amara) shows no false alarms.

 

Why it matters. The same offline system can support remote clinics and field workers on Earth where specialists and internet are unavailable.

 

Limitations (honest note). All data is simulated and calibrated to published spaceflight ranges. This is a research prototype, not a medical device. Next steps: validate on real wearable and NASA OSDR datasets, add longitudinal personalized models, and integrate an onboard medical knowledge assistant.

AI assistance: This project (code, slides and text) was developed with the help of an AI assistant (Claude by Anthropic). All data is simulated, and the risk model uses explainable statistics rather than a generative AI model.
dataRefs: NASA MSL RAD cruise radiation measurements (Zeitlin et al. 2013, Science)
